name: Alpha-lipoic acid topical

card.summary: Antioxidant applied in skin creams, studied at 5% for photoaged skin, to support a smoother, more even complexion.

quick.overview:
Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) is a compound the body makes and that is also used as an antioxidant in cosmetic creams. Topical products use it with the aim of improving the look of photoaged skin.

Research includes a randomised, placebo-controlled study of a 5% ALA cream for photoaging, and formulation work aimed at getting it into the skin; findings are limited to a few studies.
quick.how: Used as an ingredient in leave-on creams or serums within a skincare routine, often alongside other antioxidants.
quick.risks: Specific topical safety data in these sources are limited. Oral supplements are a separate use and are not covered here.

lead: Alpha-lipoic acid, also called thioctic acid, is produced in animals and serves as a cofactor for several metabolic enzymes.[1] In skincare it is used as a topical antioxidant.

People apply it hoping to improve the appearance of photoaged skin. A randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind study of a cream containing 5% ALA examined its clinical efficacy for photoaging, following earlier uncontrolled reports.[2]
Formulation research has also developed emulsions and dispersions to carry ALA into skin.[2]

angle.text: ALA creams are used with the aim of improving the appearance of sun-aged skin through antioxidant action.

paras: Wikipedia notes ALA is mostly thought to trigger the cell's oxidative-stress response rather than directly scavenge radicals, and that the article does not cover topical use.[1]

A randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind British Journal of Dermatology study (2003) tested a 5% ALA cream for photoaging; earlier uncontrolled work had suggested benefit.[2] Other publications describe liquid-crystalline dispersions and a water-in-oil emulsion of ALA for skin delivery.[2]
